name: Hydrocortisone cream

card.summary: Hydrocortisone cream is a mild topical corticosteroid that calms redness and swelling, and is used by some people on facial areas such as the nose for a smoother look.
card.note: Facial use is outside typical labelled use; steroids can thin skin with prolonged use.

quick.overview:
Hydrocortisone is a mild corticosteroid sold as a cream for eczema, allergic rashes, psoriasis and itching. It reduces inflammation, which can calm redness and swelling in treated skin.

In looksmaxxing forums some users apply it to the nose, hoping to reduce swelling and tip bulk, and others report it as a short-term, pre-event option. Reports are mixed, and no trials of that use were found.
quick.how: Users describe applying 1% cream over areas such as the nose. This is a community practice, not a labelled use. Some report results in days to weeks; one reports pimples at the application site.
quick.risks: Systemic corticosteroid effects are dose-dependent and include adrenal suppression, easy bruising and infections; long-term use is associated with osteoporosis. Wikipedia notes pregnancy safety is unclear.

lead: Hydrocortisone is a corticosteroid sold as a cream or ointment, and in most countries strengths from 0.05% to 2.5% are available without prescription.[1] It is used on allergic rashes, eczema, psoriasis and itching, where its anti-inflammatory action reduces redness and swelling in the treated skin.[1][3] That same action is the basis of its place in looksmaxxing: users hope that calming local swelling and redness will make a feature look slimmer, smoother or less inflamed.

On looksmax.org the most discussed application is the nose, where members post threads on nose-tip reduction, nose slimming and comparisons with other corticosteroids, and one thread discusses the area under the cheekbone.[2][4][5] Reports differ: some members post update threads describing results, while another describes blackheads and whiteheads and only a slight reduction in inflammation.[2][4]

Dermatology references classify 1% and 2.5% hydrocortisone as the weakest class of topical steroid, and recommend weaker steroids for thin-skinned areas such as the face.[3] No published trial has tested hydrocortisone cream for changing the shape of a nose or cheek; the research literature concerns skin disease and, for injectable or oral hydrocortisone, conditions such as septic shock and pneumonia.[1][6][7]

angle.text: Users claim a slimmer nose tip after applying 1% hydrocortisone. The labelled effect is reduced inflammation and itch in skin conditions.

infobox: Mildest class (US Class VII for 1% and 2.5%)[3]

paras: Hydrocortisone is the pharmaceutical name for cortisol, the main glucocorticoid made by the adrenal glands. As a topical medicine it is a mild corticosteroid, available as creams, ointments and lotions, usually in 0.5% to 2.5% strengths without prescription and in stronger forms by prescription.[1] Brand names for OTC creams include Cortizone and Ala-Cort.[1]

In the seven-class US potency system, hydrocortisone 1% and 2.5% sit in Class VII, the weakest group, while superpotent steroids such as clobetasol are described as up to several hundred times stronger.[3] The four-class systems used in the UK and Europe likewise place hydrocortisone 0.5 to 2.5% in the mild category.[3] Dermatology guidance cited by Wikipedia recommends weaker steroids for the face, eyelids and other thin or occluded skin.[3]

Hydrocortisone was discovered in the 1930s; a US patent was granted in 1936 and it was approved for medical use in 1941.[1] It was introduced as a US prescription medicine in 1952, and in 1979 topical hydrocortisone became available over the counter in the United States.[1] Corticosteroids as a group came into general dermatological use around 1950.[3] Hydrocortisone appears on the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines and is sold as a generic.[1]

Topical hydrocortisone treats allergic rashes, eczema, psoriasis, itching and other inflammatory skin conditions.[1] Absorption through the skin varies widely by body site, with studies reporting from about 0.5% to 14.9%, and thinner sites such as the scrotum and vulva absorbing more than the forearm.[1]

Systemic hydrocortisone, given by injection or by mouth, is a separate medical use and has been studied in intensive care. Trials have examined it in septic shock, alone or with fludrocortisone, and in severe community-acquired pneumonia.[6][7][8]

Hydrocortisone acts on glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid receptors, which regulate genes involved in inflammation and immune signalling.[1] Topically, this reduces local swelling, redness and itch in inflamed skin. Dermatology references also describe skin thinning (atrophy) and visible small blood vessels as effects of prolonged continuous steroid use, which is the reason weaker products are advised for the face.[3]

Some community members cite the idea that corticosteroids reduce collagen as a reason they expect a slimming effect on the nose; one Turkish-language thread asks whether hydrocortisone's collagen-reducing effect is a drawback for nose tip support.[9] These are members' explanations; the labelled effect of the cream is reduction of inflammation.

Looksmax.org threads on hydrocortisone cover nose-tip reduction, nose improvement, a comparison of hydrocortisone with other corticoids, a comparison with tretinoin for the nose, and a post about applying it beneath the cheekbone to make the cheekbone look more prominent.[4][5][10][14][11] Several threads are titled as before-and-after or update reports.[4][5]

Community discussion also treats hydrocortisone as part of a wider group of 'softmaxxing' options, meaning non-surgical tweaks, alongside products such as tretinoin and fat-loss approaches.[2][9] In one reply to the collagen thread, a member suggests lowering body fat and using a retinoid on the nose rather than the steroid.[9]

Users describe applying a low-strength OTC cream to the nose over days to weeks. Reported outcomes are mixed: one member who used 1% cream for about two weeks reported blackheads and whiteheads, said the reduction in inflammation was barely noticeable, and suggested at most a night-before-an-event use.[2] Other threads present positive results.[4][5] These are anecdotes, and no measurement of nose dimensions has been published.

Systemic corticosteroid effects are dose-dependent and include hypertension, fluid retention, adrenal suppression, immunosuppression and infection risk; long-term use is associated with osteoporosis, easy bruising and candidiasis.[1] Wikipedia notes that pregnancy safety is unclear for hydrocortisone, while a separate review of topical steroids reports no increased risk of miscarriage or birth defects when used as intended.[1][3]

For topical steroids on the skin, dermatology references list skin atrophy with prolonged continuous use, telangiectasia (visible small vessels), bruising, secondary fungal or bacterial infection, allergic contact dermatitis, folliculitis and facial hair growth, and perioral dermatitis.[3] They also describe tachyphylaxis, a loss of effect after several days of continuous use.[3]

Perioral dermatitis is a rash of small bumps around the mouth and nostrils. Topical steroids are the factor most strongly linked to it, and stronger steroids and longer use appear to raise the risk; stopping the steroid can initially worsen the rash.[12] It affects mostly women aged 16 to 45 but also occurs in men.[12] Application to the nose is near the area where this pattern appears.
No studies found of hydrocortisone cream for nose slimming, cheek definition or other cosmetic reshaping.

Related research concerns systemic hydrocortisone in hospital settings. The 2018 APROCCHSS trial tested hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone in adults with septic shock, and a 2024 network meta-analysis of 17 trials covering 7,688 patients compared that combination with hydrocortisone alone and with placebo or usual care.[7][8] A 2023 trial examined hydrocortisone in severe community-acquired pneumonia, and the REMAP-CAP corticosteroid domain trial of a fixed 7-day course was stopped for futility in 2025.[6][13] These studies address critical illness, not cosmetic use of the cream.

Topical hydrocortisone is OTC in the US and most countries in lower strengths, prescription-only (POM) in the UK for some forms and listed as S4 in Australia, according to Wikipedia.[1] Oral and injectable products are prescription medicines.[1]

timeline.event: Introduced as a US prescription medicine.[1]
Topical hydrocortisone becomes available over the counter in the US.[1]
NEJM trial of hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone in septic shock published.[8]
NEJM trial of hydrocortisone in severe community-acquired pneumonia published.[6]

lore.intro: Looksmax.org threads discuss low-strength hydrocortisone cream mainly for the nose and occasionally the cheek area, with some members reporting results and others reporting breakouts.[2][4][5]

claims.claim: Hydrocortisone cream slims the nose or nose tip
claims.believers: Members post update and improvement threads on nose-tip reduction after applying a 1% cream, and ask how it compares with other corticoids.[4][5][10]
claims.experts: No published studies have tested this use; labelled uses are inflammatory skin conditions.[1]

claims.claim: It is a quick pre-event option for reducing swelling
claims.believers: One user who found little lasting change suggests it might suit a night-before-an-event use.[2]
claims.experts: Dermatology references describe hydrocortisone as reducing inflammation, itch and redness in inflamed skin, and the weakest topical steroid class.[3]

claims.claim: Applying it under the cheekbone can make the cheekbone look more prominent
claims.believers: A member thread proposes hydrocortisone under the cheekbone for prominence.[11]
claims.experts: Dermatology references describe skin thinning with prolonged steroid use, and no study has tested this use.[3]

claims.claim: It clogs pores or causes whiteheads on the nose
claims.believers: One user reports blackheads and whiteheads within days and attributes it to the thick cream base.[2]
claims.experts: Dermatology references list folliculitis and perioral dermatitis among reported effects of topical steroids, particularly with prolonged use.[3][12]

claims.claim: Steroids reduce collagen, which could drop or weaken the nose tip
claims.believers: A member asking about it worries the collagen effect could make an already drooping tip worse.[9]
claims.experts: Reference texts describe skin atrophy from prolonged continuous use.[3]
